theme.name: Legal mechanism and scope of the ban
theme.claim: The ban will be implemented by amending the existing Statutory Instrument on v-notched lobsters under the Sea Fish (Conservation) Act 1967, applying to UK and Scottish vessels fishing in English waters while excluding foreign vessels due to their negligible landings.

text.line: 3.2. It is proposed that an order (SI) be made to make it an offence to fish for or land a berried lobster or crawfish in England using the power under Sections 5 and 6 of The Sea Fish (Conservation) Act 1967. ** (Reference: 1,14)

The ban would apply to all relevant British fishing vessels registered in the UK, any other relevant British fishing vessel (including those exempt from licensing requirements) and Scottish fishing vessels, fishing in English waters (0-200nm) and/or landing into English ports.
The order applies within British fishery limits excluding; Scottish waters, Northern Irish waters and territorial sea adjacent to Wales, Isle of Man, Bailiwick of Jersey and Guernsey.
We plan to implement this national ban through amending the current SI that prohibits the landing of v-notched lobsters and crawfish rather than make a new separate order. ** (Reference: 9)

The provisions of the existing order will remain the same with the new provisions on berried lobsters and crawfish added to it and applying to the same vessels currently regulated by the existing order.
This should help with the familiarisation of this new regulation and will support the Government’s agenda on simplifying the legislative landscape.
The ban wouldn’t apply to foreign vessels, as only a small amount of lobster and crawfish is landed by foreign vessels into England (only 206kg in 2014). ** (Reference: 15)
The small level of landings by foreign vessels means that the ban not applying to them shouldn’t impact the conservational benefits.

5.1. To implement this national ban, it is proposed that an amendment will made to the current SI that prohibits the landing of v-notched lobsters and crawfish rather than make a new separate order. ** (Reference: 3,9)
This will support the Government’s agenda on simplifying the legislative landscape.

theme.name: Enforcement costs and approach
theme.claim: Enforcement will rely on MMO and IFCAs using testing kits to detect scrubbed eggs, integrated into routine inspection activity at a modest estimated annual cost, with savings for IFCAs that already enforce local bans.

text.line: 4.4. In order to enforce the ban on landing berried lobsters, the MMO and IFCAs will need to invest in testing kits. ** (Reference: 1)
This is so that they can test whether lobsters have had the eggs scrubbed from their bodies to hide that they have been berried.
This testing should also be able to be applied to crawfish but costs have been based on existing testing kits for lobsters.
Each testing kit would cost around £500, and be required to be replaced annually.
There would also be an annual cost of £50 per annum per kit for replacing chemicals and other disposable materials used during testing. ** (Reference: 19)
The MMO would be required to purchase one kit per office or inspection platform and each IFCA would be required to purchase two.

As there are 12 MMO coastal offices and three inspection vessels and four IFCAs which do not currently enforce the ban on landings of berried lobsters, this results in a total annual cost to government of £11,500 to purchase the testing kits, and an annual cost of £1,150 for replacing chemicals.
4.4. There will also be additional costs to IFCAs and the MMO for training inspectors to use the testing kits. ** (Reference: 2)
This is estimated at £500 per MMO marine area for which there are four and per IFCA district for which there are four without a ban currently.
Training is assumed to need to be repeated every two years, leading to a cost every two years of £4,000.
Nevertheless, this is likely to be the highest estimate as it’s likely that costs can be reduced through conducting larger training sessions for multiple areas.
The implementation of a national ban on berried lobsters may lead to cost savings for IFCAs which already have a ban on landing berried lobsters caught within 6nm in place.
This is because IFCAs will no longer have to investigate whether any berried lobsters which are landed have been caught from within 6nm.
These savings have not been quantified.
4.4. There will be no other costs to the MMO or IFCAs for implementing or enforcing the ban. ** (Reference: 4)

This is because enforcement activities will be carried out as part of routine inspection activity (for example, checking that fishers are complying with other existing technical regulations such as minimum landing sizes) and there would be no additional or specific inspection or enforcement activity associated with the ban on landing berried lobsters.
This means that the total cost of enforcement and implementation to public bodies is £16,650 in years where training is needed and £12,650 in other years.

theme.name: Consultation to resolve outstanding design assumptions
theme.claim: Key assumptions underlying the policy's design and costings (e.g. vessel fishing locations, compliance rates, effectiveness of local bans) remain uncertain and will be tested and finalised through formal consultation and stakeholder workshops.

text.line: The consultation will ask whether respondents can provide evidence of the effects of existing local IFCA bans on landing berried lobster.
The consultation will ask for evidence of where there is evidence of the success of voluntary action by fishers.
This assumption will be tested during consultation.
The assumptions used in modelling will be tested during consultation.
The assumptions used in this analysis are discussed in Section 4, and will be tested during consultation.
The next step will be to hold a formal consultation on this proposal with an aim to for it to come into force in Tranche 1 (period to 31st December 2017).
It is also proposed that a number of regional stakeholder workshops will be held both prior and during the consultation.

To date we have extensively engaged with the MMO and IFCAs on the proposal for consideration, as well as larger stakeholders such as the Shellfish Association of Great Britain (SAGB) and National Federation of Fishemen’s Organisations (NFFO).
These organisations will be invited to participate in the stakeholder workshops.
The MMO and IFCAs will continue to be responsible for implementing this regulation and we plan to work with them and build on current procedures.
We will develop this further after the consultation in order to take into account any feedback received.

The ban would apply to all relevant British fishing vessels registered in the UK, any other relevant British fishing vessel (including those exempt from licensing requirements) and Scottish fishing vessels, fishing in English waters (0-200nm) and/or landing into English ports.
